Frequency tables and cross-tabulations

Source: R/tab.R
tab.Rd

Create Stata-style frequency tables using joint counts, separate one-way tables, or pairwise cross-tabulations:

  • tab(): Count combinations of selected variables in one long-format table with frequencies and percentages.

  • fre(): Count the same combinations as tab(), adding totals and displaying value labels.

  • tab1(): Tabulate each variable separately, returning a one-way frequency table for each variable.

  • fre1(): Tabulate each variable separately as in tab1(), adding totals and displaying value labels.

  • tab2(): Cross-tabulate every pair of selected variables, returning wide contingency tables with categories in rows and columns.

  • fre2(): Cross-tabulate every pair as in tab2(), adding marginal totals and displaying row-category labels. Column headers retain category codes.

Usage

tab(
  .data,
  ...,
  .by = NULL,
  .desc = FALSE,
  .group_order = c("keys", "frequency"),
  .total = FALSE,
  .wt = NULL,
  .wt_type = c("frequency", "analytic")
)

tab1(
  .data,
  ...,
  .by = NULL,
  .desc = FALSE,
  .type = c("list", "tibble"),
  .group_order = c("keys", "frequency"),
  .total = FALSE,
  .wt = NULL,
  .wt_type = c("frequency", "analytic")
)

tab2(
  .data,
  ...,
  .by = NULL,
  .flip = FALSE,
  .total = FALSE,
  .type = c("auto", "tibble", "flextable"),
  .wt = NULL,
  .wt_type = c("frequency", "analytic"),
  .chi2 = FALSE
)

fre2(
  .data,
  ...,
  .by = NULL,
  .flip = FALSE,
  .type = c("auto", "tibble", "flextable"),
  .wt = NULL,
  .wt_type = c("frequency", "analytic"),
  .chi2 = FALSE
)

fre(
  .data,
  ...,
  .by = NULL,
  .desc = FALSE,
  .type = c("auto", "tibble", "flextable"),
  .group_order = c("keys", "frequency"),
  .wt = NULL,
  .wt_type = c("frequency", "analytic")
)

fre1(
  .data,
  ...,
  .by = NULL,
  .desc = FALSE,
  .type = c("list", "tibble", "flextable"),
  .group_order = c("keys", "frequency"),
  .wt = NULL,
  .wt_type = c("frequency", "analytic")
)

Arguments

.data

An in-memory data frame, tibble, or data.table. tab(), tab1(), fre(), and fre1() also accept an atomic vector (without selectors or .by). Collect lazy tables first. Spatial geometry columns are excluded.

...

<tidy-select> or <data-masking> Variables to tabulate, or named expressions such as high = score >= 70. Defaults to all columns except active grouping keys. Without explicit .by, tab2() and fre2() treat inherited grouping columns as ordinary variables. Select at least two variables for cross-tabulation.

.by

<tidy-select> Optional grouping columns. For one-way and joint tables, existing dplyr::group_by() groups are inherited unless .by is supplied. tab2() and fre2() require explicit .by to create separate cross-tables for each group. Grouping keys are not tabulated.

.desc

If TRUE, sort categories by decreasing frequency within each group; missing categories remain last. Defaults to FALSE.

.group_order

Order group blocks by "keys" (default) or decreasing "frequency" (weighted totals when weights are supplied). Groups with any missing key follow complete-key groups; within each set, frequency ties follow key order. Does not change category order within groups.

.total

If TRUE, add totals, as in the corresponding fre() family function. Defaults to FALSE for tab(), tab1(), and tab2(); the fre() family always includes totals.

.wt

Optional numeric weights, given as a column or one value per row. Missing weights exclude rows; negative weights are invalid.

.wt_type

"frequency" (default) or "analytic". Frequency weights are summed as counts; analytic weights are normalized within groups. See Details for the formulas.

.type

Output form, where supported. tab() has no .type argument.

  • "list" is the default for tab1() and fre1(): one table per selected variable, retaining the input's table class where supported.

  • "auto" is the default for fre(), tab2(), and fre2(): retain the input's table class where supported.

  • "tibble" returns tibbles regardless of the input's table class. For tab1() and fre1(), it also combines the variable tables into one.

  • "flextable" returns formatted tables and requires the optional flextable package. It is available for fre(), fre1(), tab2(), and fre2(); tab2() also requires .total = TRUE.

For tab2() and fre2(), multiple pairs or explicit .by groups still produce lists; .type controls each table inside the list.

.flip

If TRUE, exchange the row and column variables in a cross-tabulation. Defaults to FALSE.

.chi2

If TRUE, report Pearson's chi-square test and Cramer's V for cross-tabulations. Analytic weights are not supported for this test.

Value

A table or list of tables, depending on the function:

  • tab() and fre() return one row per observed combination of selected categories and grouping keys, followed by n, percent, cum, valid, and valid_cum. The fre() variant adds total rows.

  • tab1() and fre1() return named lists of one-variable frequency tables. Each contains a value column and the same five statistics. Use .type = "tibble" to combine them, adding a variable column.

  • tab2() and fre2() return wide cross-tabulations: rows represent categories of one variable, columns represent categories of the other, and cells contain counts. fre2() adds marginal totals. Multiple pairs or explicit .by groups produce lists of tables.

For two selected variables, tab() and tab2() represent the same joint frequencies in different layouts: tab() provides a long table with percentages, whereas tab2() shows cell counts in a two-way table. With three or more variables, tab() counts their joint combinations, while tab2() produces a separate table for each variable pair.

Results are ungrouped and retain the input table class where supported. For non-flextable output, chi-square results are stored in the "chi2" attribute, with statistic, df, p_value, cramers_v, and n. Flextables display these results in a footer instead.

Details

Counts and percentages

The following five columns are produced by tab(), tab1(), fre(), and fre1(). For each group, let n_i be the count for category (or category combination) i, N the count across all categories, and N_valid the count excluding observations missing any measured variable. All percentages are on a 0–100 scale.

  • n: Number of observations in the category, or sum of weights if weighted.

  • percent: Percentage of all observations, 100 * n_i / N, including missing measured values in the denominator.

  • cum: Cumulative percent, summed in the displayed category order.

  • valid: Percentage of complete observations, 100 * n_i / N_valid. This is NA for categories with missing measured values.

  • valid_cum: Cumulative valid, in displayed order, omitting missing measured categories.

Thus percent corresponds to Stata's tabulate, missing, while valid uses the denominator from tabulate without missing. A missing grouping key does not by itself make a measured value invalid.

Missing values and category order

Missing measured values are kept as categories and shown last. Missingness includes NA, NaN, tagged missing values, and SPSS user-missing codes or ranges; empty strings are observed values. Factors follow their level order; other categories are sorted by value unless .desc requests frequency order. List-column elements are counted as complete values, not flattened.

Weighted counts and percentages

Let w_j be the weight for observation j in a group.

  • Frequency weights (.wt_type = "frequency"): Category counts are n_i = sum(w_j) over observations in that category. Weights need not be integers.

  • Analytic weights (.wt_type = "analytic"): Weights are rescaled within each group to sum to its number of rows. Category counts sum the rescaled weights, so the overall count stays on the sample-size scale.

  • Percentages: Both weight types give the same percentages because the normalization factor cancels in each group. Cumulative and valid percentages use the corresponding weighted counts and denominators.

Rows with missing weights are excluded; negative weights are not allowed. If ... is omitted, the weight column is not itself tabulated.

Totals and value labels

fre() and fre1() append a "Total" row within each group and may add "Valid Total" and "Missing Total" subtotals. fre2() adds a marginal total row and column. fre() and fre1() display value labels; fre2() displays row-category labels but keeps column headers based on category codes. tab() and tab1() retain underlying category codes and types. Totals may convert a category column to character or introduce a total label column. Distinct category codes remain separate even if their labels coincide.

Cross-tabulations and association tests

tab2() and fre2() report cell counts rather than the five percentages listed above. With .chi2 = TRUE, Pearson's chi-square test uses the displayed categories, including missing ones. Filter missing categories beforehand if they should not contribute to the test. Empty rows and columns are excluded from the calculation.

Let O_ij be an observed cell count, E_ij its expected count under independence, r the number of nonempty rows, c the number of nonempty columns, and N the total count:

  • Expected counts: E_ij = row_total_i * column_total_j / N.

  • Pearson's chi-square: X^2 = sum((O_ij - E_ij)^2 / E_ij).

  • Degrees of freedom: df = (r - 1) * (c - 1).

  • p-value: Upper-tail probability of a chi-square distribution with df degrees of freedom.

  • Cramer's V: sqrt(X^2 / (N * min(r - 1, c - 1))). For 2-by-2 tables, it is the signed phi coefficient, as in Stata, with the sign of O_11 * O_22 - O_12 * O_21.

Frequency weights act as cell counts for the test. Analytic weights are not supported; for complex survey designs, use survey::svychisq(). Cross-tabulation category values become column names, so conflicts with reserved names such as "total" may require recoding.

Computed variables and groups

Named expressions in ... are evaluated on ungrouped data, before counts are calculated within groups. Use grouped dplyr::mutate() first for group-specific computations. Input column names that conflict with output columns are renamed in the result; the input data are unchanged.

Examples

# Compare the three approaches using the same variables
# Joint frequencies: one long table
tab(lifeexp, region, high = lexp >= 70)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   region               high      n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <dbl+lbl>            <lgl> <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 1 [Europe & C. Asia] FALSE    12   17.6   17.6 17.6       17.6
#> 2 1 [Europe & C. Asia] TRUE     32   47.1   64.7 47.1       64.7
#> 3 2 [North America]    FALSE     6    8.82  73.5  8.82      73.5
#> 4 2 [North America]    TRUE      8   11.8   85.3 11.8       85.3
#> 5 3 [South America]    FALSE     3    4.41  89.7  4.41      89.7
#> 6 3 [South America]    TRUE      7   10.3  100   10.3      100  

# Separate one-way tables: one for region and one for high
tab1(lifeexp, region, high = lexp >= 70)
#> $region
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   value                    n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <dbl+lbl>            <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 1 [Europe & C. Asia]    44    64.7  64.7  64.7      64.7
#> 2 2 [North America]       14    20.6  85.3  20.6      85.3
#> 3 3 [South America]       10    14.7 100    14.7     100  
#> 
#> $high
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   value     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <lgl> <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 FALSE    21    30.9  30.9  30.9      30.9
#> 2 TRUE     47    69.1 100    69.1     100  
#> 

# Two-way cross-tabulation: region by high
tab2(lifeexp, region, high = lexp >= 70)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   `region \\ high`     `FALSE` `TRUE`
#>   <dbl+lbl>              <int>  <int>
#> 1 1 [Europe & C. Asia]      12     32
#> 2 2 [North America]          6      8
#> 3 3 [South America]          3      7

# Add totals and display value labels
fre(lifeexp, region)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   region               n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>            <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Europe & C. Asia    44    64.7  64.7  64.7      64.7
#> 2 North America       14    20.6  85.3  20.6      85.3
#> 3 South America       10    14.7 100    14.7     100  
#> 4 Total               68   100    NA    NA        NA  

fre2(lifeexp, region, high = lexp >= 70)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   `region \\ high` `FALSE` `TRUE` total
#>   <chr>              <int>  <int> <int>
#> 1 Europe & C. Asia      12     32    44
#> 2 North America          6      8    14
#> 3 South America          3      7    10
#> 4 total                 21     47    68

# Frequencies within groups
tab(lifeexp, high = lexp >= 70, .by = region)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   region               high      n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <dbl+lbl>            <lgl> <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 1 [Europe & C. Asia] FALSE    12    27.3  27.3  27.3      27.3
#> 2 1 [Europe & C. Asia] TRUE     32    72.7 100    72.7     100  
#> 3 2 [North America]    FALSE     6    42.9  42.9  42.9      42.9
#> 4 2 [North America]    TRUE      8    57.1 100    57.1     100  
#> 5 3 [South America]    FALSE     3    30    30    30        30  
#> 6 3 [South America]    TRUE      7    70   100    70       100  

# Continuous variables: count each distinct value, then shorten the display
tab(lifeexp, lexp) |> print_headtail(n = 6)
#> # A tibble: 20 × 6
#>     lexp     n percent    cum valid valid_cum
#>    <dbl> <int>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1    57     1    1.47   1.47  1.47      1.47
#>  2    61     1    1.47   2.94  1.47      2.94
#>  3    62     2    2.94   5.88  2.94      5.88
#>  ⋮     ⋮     ⋮     ⋮      ⋮     ⋮         ⋮  
#> 18    77     5    7.35  85.3   7.35     85.3 
#> 19    78     4    5.88  91.2   5.88     91.2 
#> 20    79     6    8.82 100     8.82    100   
#> # ... 14 rows omitted in the middle; use print(x, n = Inf) to show all rows.

tab(lifeexp, lexp) |> print_interval(n = 6)
#> # A tibble: 20 × 6
#>     lexp     n percent    cum valid valid_cum
#>    <dbl> <int>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1    57     1    1.47   1.47  1.47      1.47
#>  5    64     3    4.41  11.8   4.41     11.8 
#>  9    68     3    4.41  25     4.41     25   
#> 12    71     6    8.82  47.1   8.82     47.1 
#> 16    75     4    5.88  72.1   5.88     72.1 
#> 20    79     6    8.82 100     8.82    100   
#> # ... 14 rows omitted between displayed positions; use print(x, n = Inf) to
#> # show all rows.

# Pearson's chi-square and Cramer's V
result <- tab2(lifeexp, region, high = lexp >= 70, .chi2 = TRUE)
#> Pearson chi2(2) = 1.2127   Pr = 0.545
#> Cramer's V = 0.1335
attr(result, "chi2")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   statistic    df p_value cramers_v     n
#>       <dbl> <int>   <dbl>     <dbl> <int>
#> 1      1.21     2   0.545     0.134    68

# Frequency weights
survey <- tibble::tibble(response = c("yes", "no", "yes"), w = c(2, 1, 3))
tab(survey, response, .wt = w)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   response     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>    <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 no           1    16.7  16.7  16.7      16.7
#> 2 yes          5    83.3 100    83.3     100
